article_text:
The charges against Amazon’s epic (and epically priced) “Lord of the Rings” series, “The Rings of Power,” stacked up quickly. The first two seasons were pretty good by blockbuster standards — and I wasn’t alone in saying so — but the record-breaking costs, as well as the franchise’s lofty pedigree, set expectations higher than Great Eagles can soar. When the most expensive TV series ever made struggled to yield the requisite viewership spikes and comparable cultural impact, the claws came out.

Showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay’s series was, among other prominent complaints, a lackluster imitation of Peter Jackson’s films and an all-too-obvious ploy to become TV’s next “Game of Thrones.” Even when the visuals wowed, the characters weren’t memorable enough (save for the dwarves), the stories weren’t fun enough (again, except for the dwarves), and the twists weren’t smart enough. (The dwarves, in their infinite wisdom, did not partake.) Perhaps most damning for a show paid and made for an audience of one, Jeff Bezos’ pet project didn’t get J.R.R. Tolkien’s text — at least, not on at any depth .

On the whole, these criticisms weren’t enough to spoil a flawed but ambitious saga. Sure, “The Rings of Power” was made with too much deference to the past and too little innovation for the present — repeating itself (and other “Lord of the Rings” adaptations) while lacking the deft touch and sweeping imagination viewers crave from their greatest fantasy series. But it was still thrilling in its spectacle, from sets to sound design, costumes to vivid colors. (“House of the Dragon” it was not. ) Episodes easily conveyed the filmmakers’ giddy excitement for the next big battle scene, the next big twist, and the next big moment in their Tolkien translation. All that money was on the screen, where it belonged, and dreams of spending it elsewhere — like, say, on many shows instead of just one — were set aside when Mount Doom erupted and the Siege of Eregion was underway.

I say all this, dear reader, not just as a handy recap of where things stand for yet another series with lengthy breaks between seasons, but to establish my position on a franchise that’s reached its sudden, somewhat unexpected nadir ( for now , at least). While flaws were evident before, “The Rings of Power” Season 3 is undone by them. The listless episodes aren’t just hamstrung by additional exposition and a dearth of deadly combat; there’s a lingering wariness to it all, as if the filmmakers have run out of surprises and settled for treating their adaptation like the supplementary material it’s based on.

The third season begins with a recap of its own: Five years have passed since the Elven city of Eregion fell, and Sauron (Charlie Vickers) controls more of Middle Earth than ever. His army of orcs are tracking down the rest of the titular rings, which are safe(ish) with the elves in the luxe strongholds of Lindon and Rivendell, as well as my beloved dwarves in the sonorous mines of Khazad-dûm. But the Dark Lord himself is right where we left him, trying to forge the one ring to rule them all. Celembrimbor (Charles Edwards) was the only Elf who knew how to forge it, and now that he’s dead, Sauron grows more desperate by the day.

Not that you could tell from Vickers’ affectless portrayal. In “The Rings of Power,” the Australian actor is saddled with an arguably impossible task: Take the very presence of evil — which Tolkien so profoundly established in readers’ limitless imaginations as “an image of malice and hatred,” before Jackson sagely (and cinematically) channeled that energy into a giant, all-seeing eye — and embody that transcendent menace within a guy who looks like the guitarist next door . Vickers was able to hide his Sauron in plain sight during Season 1, when no one knew who Halbrand really was, but the big reveal didn’t lead to a bigger (or more sinister) performance, and attempts to lend human dimensions to evil incarnate similarly suffered.

What Sauron means to the series is more powerful than what he does on a scene-by-scene basis, and Season 3 throws that balance way out of whack. Absent significant conflict elsewhere, the story keeps returning to Sauron and his schemes, but none of his scenes have enough juice to elevate him to adequate levels of intimidation. A lengthy climactic sequence near the end of the season deploys shifting aspect ratios, operatic music cues, and dead-eyes stares aplenty, but they don’t add up to the riveting spectacle its creators intended. Instead, they only remind audiences how little Season 3 has to show off, not to mention how misguided some of those showcases can get.

Númenor, with its warring cousins Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) and Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle), remains a bland, human-centered snooze-fest. (My god , these people are boring.) The desert empire of Rhûn fares slightly better with Ciarán Hinds’ Dark Wizard (those eyebrows!), but the man long known and now confirmed as Gandalf (Daniel Weyman) is still little more than a mysterious symbol. (Just wait ’til you see him… put on his hat?)

And what’s become of Prince Durin (Owain Arthur), Princess Disa (Sophia Nomvete), and my rambunctious, sunless dwarves? You’d think lifelong cave dwellers would thrive in a season that’s lost a considerable amount of its light (times are tough in Middle Earth, and “The Rings of Power” has never been subtle), but my feisty friends are stuck in a plot so predictable it’s all but spelled out in the very first episode by accident! (When the wisest dwarf speaks, we all know to listen.)

New additions feel slotted in, as if emotional attachments are expected to emerge from name recognition alone (sorry to Celeborn, Galadriel’s long-lost hubby), while old favorites are nowhere to be found. (Nori and Poppy are entirely absent through seven episodes.) Others that do show up aren’t developed thoroughly enough to support their dramatic turns, like the Southlands boy turned tree-chopping, Mordor-enslaved man Theo (Tyroe Muhafidin), or get wasted in order to prop up other, less compelling characters, like Arondir (Ismael Cruz Córdova).

Perhaps “The Rings of Power” Season 3 is just a temporary dip — the midway point of a five-season plan that needs to set the table so we can feast for the two final seasons. Even if that’s the case, it’s no excuse. “The Lord of the Rings” may engender enough goodwill to give “The Rings of Power” a little leeway, but a full season lacking in evident ingenuity and attentive investment is enough to strip away the nostalgic sheen.

The biggest slight against the series has always been its status as a prequel: Based on appendices to “The Lord of the Rings,” this is the story the movies ran through as an epilogue, so it’s going to take a little extra sumthin’ sumthin’ to prove expanding into a five-season series is warranted. Instead, we’re given the same ol’, same ol’. Not everything needs to be realized onscreen just for the sake of seeing it happen, step by step, beat by beat, ring by ring. Yet bearing witness to the inevitable is Season 3’s greatest ambition.

Grade: C

“The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power” premieres Wednesday, November 11 on Amazon Prime Video with four episodes. Two episodes will be released November 18 and 25 to complete the season.

article_text:
Quanto conta il luogo da cui proveniamo nella costruzione della nostra identità? E come possiamo custodire le nostre radici senza trasformarle in un confine? Sono alcune delle domande al centro di Grazia Ritrovata , il progetto dedicato a Grazia Deledda che arricchisce la stagione culturale 2026 di Rebeccu Arte , in Sardegna, in provincia di Sassari , sotto la direzione artistica di Valeria Orani , nel centenario del conferimento del Premio Nobel per la Letteratura alla scrittrice sarda.

Tra le protagoniste del programma figura Sonita Sarker , docente emerita di Women’s, Gender, and Sexuality Studies e di Letteratura inglese al Macalester College, in Minnesota. Studiosa di teorie femministe e postcoloniali, Sarker ha dedicato importanti ricerche a Deledda, analizzando il rapporto tra appartenenza geografica, identità nazionale e modernità.

Nel saggio Grazia Deledda: From Island to Continent and Never Back Again , contenuto nel volume Women Writing Race, Nation, and History: N/native , la studiosa interpreta la Sardegna non come periferia culturale, ma come osservatorio privilegiato da cui mettere in discussione le narrazioni dominanti e ripensare il rapporto tra centro e margine.

Il 28 e 29 ottobre Sarker sarà nel Meilogu per affiancare la drammaturga Nalini Vidoolah Mootoosamy nel laboratorio Tradurre il sentimento . Attraverso brevi testi deleddiani, i partecipanti esploreranno le possibilità della traduzione come pratica creativa, capace di attraversare lingue, memorie ed esperienze personali. Un’occasione per interrogare anche il significato contemporaneo di migrazione, genere e appartenenza.

Il percorso culminerà a New York, il 10 e 11 dicembre 2026, con due appuntamenti internazionali. Il Martin E. Segal Theatre Center del CUNY Graduate Center ospiterà un symposium dedicato alla scrittrice, mentre alla Casa Italiana Zerilli-Marimò della New York University sarà proiettato Quasi Grazia , film di Peter Marcias .

Prodotto da 369gradi, Grazia Ritrovata costruisce così un dialogo tra comunità locali e ricerca internazionale, restituendo alla letteratura di Deledda una dimensione contemporanea. Dalla Sardegna agli Stati Uniti, il progetto ribalta l’idea di periferia: l’isola diventa il punto di partenza per ripensare identità, memoria e libertà di appartenenza.

article_text:
Pop Art arrived in the middle of the 20th century, as artists experimented with pictures and processes borrowed from mass media. Their high-low mashups, nostalgic references, and high-octane colors remain alluring, relevant, and surprisingly misunderstood. In time for the Whitney Museum of American Art’s retrospective on Roy Lichtenstein, read these five books to revisit the significant cultural movement and track its continual reinvention.

The Long March of Pop: Art, Music, and Design 1930–1995 Art movements tend to be situated as hard breaks with their immediate past, but great art historians address how a movement is drawn out of the world it inherits. In The Long March of Pop , Thomas Crow argues that Pop artists were forged in post-World War II classrooms that welcomed a surge of veterans and explored the “image worlds” of American folk art as source material. He organizes the text with chapters on key artists (Robert Indiana, James Rosenquist, and Robert Rauschenberg among them), but his analysis radiates out to include Americana treasures from surfboards to Woody Guthrie songs.

Seductive Subversion: Women Pop Artists 1958–1968 Appraisals of Pop art’s visual characteristics rapidly and narrowly consolidated around men, forcing women artists to the margins of the movement’s propulsive trajectory. Seductive Subversion provides exacting observations of how the art world excluded such artists as Pauline Boty, Faith Ringgold, and Marjorie Strider, who fit the formal cues of Pop art so precisely that one is reminded of rampant sexism and racism as well. But where this catalog for a traveling exhibition in 2010 really shines is when it cracks open the canon to argue for the Pop sensibilities of artists like Chryssa, Lee Lozano, and Alina Szapocznikow, who have largely been claimed by historians of other movements and styles.

International Pop Pop art is replete with images of consumer goods that, as this catalog for a 2015 Walker Art Center exhibition reminds us, circulate in a global marketplace. The rigorously researched compendium of essays, with a stellar timeline, dives deep into nation-specific histories of Pop from countries spanning the Americas, Asia, and Europe while also seriously considering the implications of the movement’s rise alongside American economic domination. This book is careening, festive, and incisive, bringing together a number of artists still overdue for solo museum shows. (Plus, Walker Art Center publications are always worth picking up for the design alone.)

This shift reflects a set of concerns that remain relevant today, from the role of the artist in society to technological innovations’ impact on how we picture the world. Michael Lobel’s 2002 book sets itself apart in illuminating how such narratives surface in Roy Lichtenstein’s art, including an in-depth account of what is one of Pop art’s more fascinating origin stories. See: Lichtenstein’s training at Ohio State University’s “flash lab,” where students drew images that were screened in a blackout room for one-tenth of a second, effectively turning the body into a mechanical recording device.

Andy Warhol Exhibits: A Glittering Alternative Retail culture made its way into Pop art imagery and also influenced how artists and curators installed work, pulling inspiration from department store windows and marketing displays. This publication accompanied a 2020 exhibition in Vienna that focused on Andy Warhol’s approach, from maximalist wallpapers to towers of Brillo boxes. Come for the fascinating archival photographs but stay for the book’s last essay, by Jennifer Sichel: a groundbreaking reconsideration of Warhol’s conception of homosexuality based on recently discovered tapes of an early interview he did with the chronically underknown critic Gene Swenson. In Warhol’s intriguing appraisal, Pop art transcends a mere exploration of the consumer landscape into a radical field of queer desire. (Sichel also wrote Criticism Without Authority , a book focusing on Swenson and fellow queer critic Jill Johnston, published just last year.)

article_text:
2026年、約4年間の休館を経て生まれ変わった江戸東京博物館。建物の設備を更新するだけでなく、常設展示にも大きく手を入れ、江戸から現代の東京までの歴史を、より身近に体験できる空間へと進化しました。インタビュー後編では、引き続き事業企画課長の新田太郎さんに、改修後の取り組みや11月28日から始まるリニューアル記念特別展「円山応挙 リアルの先へ 空間革命」の見どころなどを伺いました。

「見る」から「入る」へ――歴史を浴びる新しい常設展示

――今回のリニューアルで、常設展示室はどのように新しくなったのでしょうか。

新田 最も大きく変わったのは、復元された江戸・東京の街並みや建物を、外から眺めるだけでなく、実際にその中に入って体験できる場所を大幅に増やしたことです。江戸博はもともと実物大の復元展示や精巧な模型が特徴でしたが、リニューアルを機に、さらに展示室全体の配置や導線を見直し、より深く歴史の世界に入り込めるように工夫しました。

――たとえば、どのあたりの展示が大きく変わったのでしょうか？

新田 江戸ゾーンでは、例えば「江戸の長屋」です。開館当初は二部屋分を切り取ったような展示でしたが、約10年前の改修で5部屋を再現し、今回さらに、そのうちの1部屋に靴を履いたまま入れるようにしました。長屋の路地を歩き、室内に入って、当時の暮らしを実際の身体感覚で味わっていただけます。また、歌舞伎の芝居小屋「中村座」の廊下は通り抜けられるようになりました。

――芝居小屋は、中にずっと入りたいなと思っていたので、個人的にも念願がかないました！東京ゾーンでも同じような工夫がされているのでしょうか。

新田 例えば、建築史家で建築家でもある藤森館長に監修いただき、今回、史実に基づき「朝野新聞社」から改築した「初代服部時計店」は、26メートルあるファサードの入口部分を通れるようにいたしました。また、「同潤会アパートメント」の復元展示を新設したのですが、頃合いを見て、サポートスタッフの案内で内部にも入れるよう準備を進めています。

――より人々の暮らしがリアルに体感できそうですよね。

新田 そうですね。私はよく「歴史を浴びていただきたい」と言うのですが、今回のリニューアルでは、まさにそうした「没入感」を一段と高めることを意識しています。

――リニューアル後、江戸ゾーンには美術館のような落ち着いた展示空間もできましたね。

新田 展示室を歩いていると、どうしても巨大な模型や映像などに目を奪われがちですが、江戸博の常設展示室には常時約2000点の文化財資料も展示されており、絵画、染織、工芸、古文書、写真、印刷物、民具など多彩な資料は保護のため、材質に応じて 、1か月から３か月おきなどと、定期的に入れ替えています。今回のリニューアルを機に、浮世絵版画など美術作品としての価値を有する資料については、作品と静かに向き合えるギャラリーのような空間を設けました。ぜひ、江戸博の誇る名品の魅力にも触れてみていただければと思っています。

言葉も年齢も障害も越えて――「街中に江戸博を蒔きたい」

――リニューアルした江戸博で、常設展示や特別展のほかにも、ぜひ立ち寄ってほしいおすすめの場所はありますか。

新田 実は、展示室以外にも見ていただきたい場所がたくさんあるんです。例えば、7階の図書室は今回のリニューアルでスペースを拡充しました。江戸や東京の歴史・文化に関する専門書だけでなく、子ども向けの本も充実させています。『ねこねこ日本史』のようなマンガ仕立ての歴史の本や、昔の生活道具を紹介する本などもありますので、ご家族でも気軽に利用していただければと思います。

――7階には、東京の街を一望できる眺めのよい場所もあるそうですね。

新田 図書室の手前、エレベーターホールに「本の広場」という休憩スペースがあって、実はここが館内でも数少ない眺望スポットなんです。お台場方面や新宿の高層ビル群が見渡せて、天気がよければ房総半島の方まで望むことができます。私自身、初めて江戸博を訪れたとき、長いエスカレーターであれだけ高いところまで上がるのだから、きっと素晴らしい眺めが楽しめるだろうと期待してがっかりした記憶があります（笑）。ですから、ここはぜひ多くの方に知っていただきたいですね。もちろん無料でご利用いただけます。

――高床式の巨大な建物の下に広がる、3階の「江戸東京ひろば」は、どのように活用されていくのでしょうか？

新田 今回のリニューアルでは、館の魅力を向上させるために、建築家の重松象平さんに各所の空間演出をしていただきました。そこで登場したものの一つが、ひろばの天井と柱を巨大スクリーンに見立てた映像です。曜日や時間帯は限られますが、夕方から夜にかけ投影する取り組みも行っています。約4000㎡の巨大映像の迫力を是非とも楽しんでいただきたいです。 （※上映日は毎月公式HPにて発表）

――プロジェクションマッピング以外にも、ここ最近の江戸東京博物館ではデジタル技術を展示に積極的に活用されているイメージがあります。

新田 江戸博では、コロナ禍を契機にデジタル技術の活用を加速させ、2022年からの長期休館中には、実際の展示室に代わって江戸・東京の歴史や文化を体験できるゲームアプリ「 ハイパー江戸博 」シリーズを展開してきました。リニューアル開館後は、そこで培った技術やノウハウを生かし、現実の展示空間とデジタル技術を融合させたXR体験へと発展させています。2026年7月には、スマホ上で実際の展示物にAR（拡張現実）やVR（仮想現実）を重ねて楽しめる無料のアプリ「 ハイパー江戸博 XRミュージアム 」を公開しました。

――とてもおもしろそうですね。具体的には、どのように楽しめばよいのでしょうか？

新田 お手元のスマホにアプリをインストールしていただき、アプリ上のカメラ機能を使って、館内各所に設けられた専用マーカーを読み取っていただきます。たとえば、館内の日本橋の付近に設置されたマーカーを読み取ると、画面に江戸時代の日本橋の風景などが現れます。常設展示室には、全部で30のマーカーが用意されていますので、ぜひ、頑張ってすべて制覇していただければと思います。さらに、博物館の外でもこのアプリを楽しめるようになっています。

――館内だけじゃなくて、館外でも楽しめるんですね？

新田 そうなんです。銀座や日本橋、両国、浅草などの指定された場所に行ってスマホをかざすと、現在の街並みに昔の風景を重ねて見ることができます。例えば銀座四丁目の交差点では、現在の和光の建物にかつての服部時計店の姿が重なり、両国橋では江戸時代の花火を眺めたりできます。日本橋では弥次さん喜多さんに出会うこともできます。博物館で歴史を学んで終わりではなく、実際に街を歩きながら、その場所の過去を体感できるわけです。こうした仕掛けをどんどん増やして、「もっと街中に江戸博を蒔いていきたい」と思っています。

大乗寺の「三つの間」が出現――「円山応挙」展と江戸博の楽しみ方

――11月28日からは、リニューアル記念特別展「円山応挙 リアルの先へ 空間革命」が開幕します。初期から晩年まで、初公開作品や、海外からの里帰りとなる貴重な作品など、120点を超える作品が集結します。特に注目してほしい見どころはどこでしょうか。

新田 最大の見どころは、兵庫県の大乗寺に伝わる応挙晩年の傑作がやってくることですね。大乗寺は「応挙寺」とも呼ばれ、応挙が晩年に手がけた障壁画で知られています。今回は作品を一枚ずつ鑑賞していただくだけではなく、本来の建築空間と一体になった絵画として、その魅力を味わっていただける展示になります。

――具体的には、どのような展示方法になるのでしょうか。

新田 大乗寺にある「孔雀の間」「芭蕉の間」「山水の間」という三つの部屋を、実際の障壁画を用いて展示室内に再現します。来館者の皆さんには、それぞれの部屋を巡るように鑑賞していただくわけです。まさに大乗寺そのものが江戸博にやってくるような感じですね。応挙は写実的な絵を描くだけでなく、部屋全体を一つの絵画空間として構成した画家でもあります。その空間に身を置き、応挙が生み出した世界を体感していただきたいですね。

――最後に、これから江戸博を訪れる読者に向けてメッセージをお願いします。

新田 楽しみ方はいろいろあります。特別展で旬の展示をご覧いただくほかに、 常設展示で歴史を体感するのもいいですし、図書室を利用したり、広い「江戸東京ひろば」で過ごしたりするのもいい。無料で通り抜けられる場所もありますし、建物の上の方から街を眺められる休憩場所もあります。まずは散歩しに来ていただきたいですね。何かを勉強しなくちゃと構えるより、ふらっと来て、歩き回ってみる。そうすると、きっと何か新しい発見があると思います。

article_text:
La nueva adaptación de Carrie, dirigida por Mike Flanagan, llega a Prime Video y vuelve a poner sobre la mesa las similitudes entre el personaje de Stephen King y Once, de Stranger Things. El director explicó por qué la comparación debe entenderse en otro sentido.

Mike Flanagan llega a Prime Video con una nueva adaptación de Carrie , la clásica novela de Stephen King publicada en 1974. La historia vuelve a centrarse en Carrie White , una adolescente con poderes telequinéticos que debe enfrentarse al acoso de sus compañeros y a una vida familiar marcada por el fanatismo religioso. Sin embargo, desde que se conocieron los primeros detalles de la serie, las redes sociales comenzaron a encontrar similitudes entre Carrie y Stranger Things , especialmente por la presencia de una protagonista con poderes sobrenaturales. Para Flanagan, la comparación tiene un punto de partida equivocado.

La razón es sencilla: Carrie apareció mucho antes que la serie creada por los hermanos Duffer. De hecho, Stephen King publicó su primera novela más de cuatro décadas antes del estreno de Stranger Things en Netflix , en 2016.

La influencia de Carrie sobre la cultura popular tampoco es nueva. El personaje de King marcó a numerosas historias posteriores que exploraron la adolescencia, el aislamiento, el bullying y el despertar de poderes sobrenaturales. Stranger Things no es una excepción.

Mike Flanagan habló sobre las comparaciones entre Carrie y Stranger Things

Durante una entrevista con Screen Rant, Mike Flanagan fue consultado por las comparaciones que comenzaron a surgir entre Carrie y Stranger Things. El director explicó que, a la hora de desarrollar esta nueva adaptación, tuvieron en cuenta las distintas versiones que ya existen de la historia, pero también aquellos personajes que fueron influenciados por la creación de Stephen King.

“Para mí, no tiene sentido intentar hacer un remake y repetir lo que ya se ha hecho. Eso implicaba tener en cuenta no solo las adaptaciones anteriores, sino también, como bien dices, a Once y a otros personajes que, obviamente, están fuertemente influenciados por Carrie White”.

De esta manera, Flanagan dejó claro que Once no representa una referencia previa a Carrie, sino todo lo contrario. El personaje interpretado por Millie Bobby Brown forma parte de una larga lista de protagonistas que, de una u otra manera, recibieron la influencia de Carrie White.

La comparación tampoco resulta extraña desde el punto de vista visual o conceptual. Ambas historias presentan a jóvenes con habilidades sobrenaturales que deben aprender a lidiar con sus poderes mientras atraviesan situaciones de violencia y aislamiento. La diferencia fundamental está en el origen de esos poderes y, por supuesto, en el contexto de cada relato.

Carrie, una historia que sigue influyendo décadas después

Publicada en 1974, Carrie fue la primera novela publicada de Stephen King y rápidamente se convirtió en uno de los títulos más importantes de su carrera. Dos años después, Brian De Palma llevó la historia al cine con una película protagonizada por Sissy Spacek, considerada hasta hoy como una de las grandes adaptaciones de la obra del escritor.

Desde entonces, Carrie tuvo nuevas versiones y continuó dejando su huella en el género. Su influencia también puede encontrarse en numerosas producciones posteriores que abordaron el acoso escolar, la adolescencia y personajes jóvenes con capacidades extraordinarias.

En el caso de Stranger Things, los propios hermanos Duffer han reconocido en distintas oportunidades la influencia de Stephen King en su trabajo. La serie de Netflix combina además diferentes elementos del cine y la literatura de terror y ciencia ficción de las décadas de 1970 y 1980.

Por eso, para Flanagan, el desafío de esta nueva versión de Carrie no consiste en ignorar esas influencias, sino en reconocerlas y encontrar una manera diferente de contar una historia que ya forma parte de la cultura popular.

article_text:
Donnie Dunagan, who voiced Bambi in the Walt Disney classic, as well as playing the son of Frankenstein opposite Basil Rathbone and Boris Karloff, has died aged 92.

Dunagan was six when he was chosen to provide the voice of the young deer in the animation’s most heartbreaking chapter. He recalled the experience in the recording booth as easy and relaxed, with rudimentary technology and notes from an assistant director instructing him to pretend his own mother had died when voicing Bambi’s reaction to his mother being killed by a hunter.

The actor recalled that Bambi’s mother originally dies on screen, but Disney altered this in the edit. Nonetheless, Dunagan received considerable hate mail from the hunting community afterwards.

Bambi, whose release was delayed in the wake of the attack on Pearl Harbor, ended up being Dunagan’s final film. He began his career on horror films Son of Frankenstein and Tower of London, playing the curly blond-haired son of Rathbone’s Dr Frankenstein, as well as featuring in films such as Mother Carey’s Chickens, The Forgotten Woman, Vigil in the Night and Meet the Chump.

He recalled often playing checkers with Karloff on set, while the latter was in full makeup dressed as the monster.

After college, Dunagan joined the military in 1952 where he spent 25 years and for which he was awarded a bronze star and three Purple Hearts for bravery. He never disclosed his early career to his comrades, but said that “one of the biggest regrets of my life is that I didn’t have the courage to tell my close personal friends in the Marine Corps that I had been a part of the wonderful work of Mr Disney”.

In 2015, he reflected on the experience by calling it “pure joy that both children and 80-year-olds can enjoy the film together. I could be working in the White House and children couldn’t care less. But let someone say, ‘that dude over there was the face or voice of Bambi’, and I am an immediate adopted grandfather to them. That is just an unmatchable joy, and a real responsibility.”

article_text:
Dans l’histoire du cinéma français, René Vautier a tracé sa route en totale indépendance, loin des voies officielles. Il est sans aucun doute le cinéaste ayant eu le plus affaire à la censure, et ce, dès son premier film, le court métrage Afrique 50 (1950), qui détourne une commande de la Ligue française de l’enseignement pour dénoncer les crimes commis par l’armée française au Niger, généralement présenté comme le premier film français anticolonialiste.

Mais voilà qu’aux interdictions de diffusion et aux emprisonnements connus de son vivant, se prolonge aujourd’hui, plus de dix ans après sa mort, une lutte politique pour l’effacement de son œuvre. Plusieurs événements distincts, survenus presque simultanément, attestent de ces faits. D’une part, en septembre dernier, la municipalité RN d’Elne (Pyrénées­-Orientales) a débaptisé le cinéma qui portait son nom, le maire d’extrême droite Steve Fortel jugeant la référence trop « politique » ; une pétition contestant cette décision a déjà recueilli près de seize mille voix, aussi soutenue par de nombreux acteurs de l’industrie (l’AFCAE, l’ACID, le GNCR…) et salles de cinéma partout en France, temporairement renommées « René-Vautier » pour l’occasion.

D’autre part, la ressortie à l’automne du documentaire Octobre à Paris de Jacques Panijel, qui montre la répression raciste et meurtrière contre les Algériens lors de la manifestation parisienne du 17 octobre 1961, un film censuré pendant douze ans avant qu’il n’obtienne son visa d’exploitation en 1973 grâce à la grève de la faim de René Vautier. En guise de solidarité, les séances seront précédées du court métrage Le Remords, réalisé par Vautier en 1974. Mais, si ce nom suscite encore aujourd’hui autant de haine et d’acharnement, c’est parce que son œuvre, à la fois politique et cinématographique, dénonce une histoire profondément raciste et autoritaire.

Une contre-histoire

Comment un Finistérien, né en 1928, a-t-il pu croiser la route du FLN (le Front de libération nationale, parti politique algérien fondé en 1954, qui a lutté contre la colonisation française jusqu’à l’indépendance du pays, en 1962, et a ensuite gouverné jusqu’en 1989) une trentaine d’années plus tard ? La vie débordante d’aventures et de déconvenues de René Vautier semble s’être écrite dans l’ombre de la V e République : elle commence véritablement dans la Résistance (il n’a même pas 16 ans), où le lycéen de Quimper forge ses valeurs, récompensées d’une croix de guerre remise par le général de Gaulle en personne. Un peu par hasard, il se retrouve à l’IDHEC (ancien nom de La Fémis), dont il sort premier.

Commence alors pour lui une vie de voyages et de contestation, passée à critiquer et à faire connaître les injustices commises au nom du peuple français tout au long de la seconde moitié du xx e siècle : dès 1950, dans les colonies françaises d’Afrique de l’Ouest, mais aussi auprès des dockers de Brest ( Un homme est mort, 1950, film perdu), des luttes féministes ( Quand les femmes ont pris la colère, 1977, coréalisé avec Soazig Chappedelaine-Vautier), ou contre l’extrême droite ( À propos de… l’autre détail, en 1984). Fleurissent aussi, au milieu de sa filmographie, bon nombre d’œuvres réalisées à plusieurs mains : avec la réalisatrice Nicole Le Garrec ( La Folle de Toujane, 1974 ; Quand tu disais Valéry, 1975) ; ( Classe de lutte, 1969) avec les ouvriers du Groupe Medvedkine, Chris Marker… Au-delà de la fibre radicalement militante des films de René Vautier, il ne faut pas passer à côté d’une œuvre tout aussi poétique : de manière très littérale dans son film Et le mot frère et le mot camarade (1995), réalisé à partir de poèmes de résistants ; des textes toujours inspirés, débordants de vie et d’images, qu’il récite en voix off dans nombre de ses films ; mais aussi, plus généralement, dans sa façon de saisir des détails et d’ériger des vies minuscules ou disparues en grands sujets de cinéma. Sa filmographie a quelquefois emprunté des détours fictionnels, et pas des moindres : il se donne le rôle principal du court métrage Le Remords, film ô combien actuel, dans lequel il pointe l’irresponsabilité des cinéastes qui ne filment pas le présent immédiat.

Et puis il y aura l’Algérie, dont il assistera, du premier rang, à la sanglante indépendance. Les films qu’il y tourne sont ses plus connus : Avoir 20 ans dans les Aurès en 1972, par exemple, une œuvre très critique du comportement des soldats français en Algérie, sans oublier Un peuple en marche sorti en 1963, sorte de bilan de la guerre d’Algérie servant aussi de passation entre Vautier et toute une génération de cinéastes algériens qu’il a formés au Centre audiovisuel d’Alger, dont il est le fondateur. C’est cet engagement sans concessions du côté des opprimés qui lui vaut aujourd’hui les foudres de l’extrême droite, qui a vite fait de le réduire à un « soutien du FLN ». On préférera se plonger dans les Mémoires magnifiques du principal intéressé, Caméra citoyenne (1998, Apogée), pour découvrir les subtilités et les évolutions dans les rapports entretenus par Vautier avec le parti politique algérien. Un ouvrage indispensable, aussi beau livre de contre-histoire que bible cinéphile poétique, pratique, technique et curieuse, dont on espère une réédition prochaine. La majorité de ses films est disponible sur l’excellente plateforme de streaming Cinémutins. Tout un programme pour l’année à venir !

article_text:
19世紀の初期写真術から現代の実験的な写真技法までを紹介する展覧会「写真術の系譜―初期写真技法から実験的オルタナティブへ―」が、2026年11月20日（金）から2027年1月27日（水）まで、東京・中野の東京工芸大学 写大ギャラリーで開催される。

本展では、ダゲレオタイプ（銀板写真）やアルビューメンプリント（鶏卵紙）、プラチナパラジウムプリントなど、写真史を形づくってきた多様な技法に着目。ウジェーヌ・アジェ、エドワード・スタイケン、アーヴィング・ペン、安井仲治、新井卓ら国内外の作家による約45点を通して、写真表現と技術の変遷をたどる。

展示は、現代のオルタナティブプロセス研究を牽引するマイク・ウェアの作品から始まる。続いて、アジェによるパリの街並みを捉えた鶏卵紙プリント、エドワード・カーティスのオロトーン、スタイケンのフォトグラヴュール、ペンのプラチナパラジウムプリントなどを紹介。それぞれの技法が生み出す独特の階調や質感、光の表現を比較できる構成となっている。

さらに、梅阪鶯里やノーマン・ロックス、ピエール・コルディエらによる実験的な作品も展示。デジタルプリントが主流となった現在、デジタルネガと伝統的な印画技法を組み合わせるなど、新たな展開を見せるオルタナティブプロセスの可能性にも光を当てる。

article_text:
Thailand’s and Nepal’s Oscar submissions, “ 9 Temples to Heaven ” and “ Elephants in the Fog ,” are among 10 titles competing at the 27th edition of Tokyo Filmex , which will run Nov. 20–29 in the Japanese capital’s Yurakucho district.

Taiwanese actor Lee Kang-sheng , who has appeared in every feature by auteur Tsai Ming-liang since “Rebels of the Neon God” in 1992, will sit on the three-member international jury. Additional jurors will be named later. The panel will pick a Grand Prize winner, whose director will receive JPY700,000 ($4,500), and a Special Jury Prize winner, whose director will receive JPY300,000 ($1,900). Both awards will be handed out at a ceremony on Nov. 29.

Related Stories

Korean Webtoon Adaptations, ‘The Vanishing Act’ Lead 2027 Vertical Slate Unveiled by COL Group, V47 and Virtue Asia

‘Pixels and Pencils’ Panelists Talk the Dangers of AI, Demanding Animation Processes and the Importance of Human Creativity

The competition is open to emerging Asian directors with films finished in 2025 or 2026. Four of this year’s selections are first features.

Sompot Chidgasornpongse, who has worked as assistant director to Thai filmmaker Apichatpong Weerasethakul, makes his narrative debut with “9 Temples to Heaven.” The deadpan family comedy follows a 63-year-old man who drags nine relatives on a one-day tour of nine temples after a fortune teller warns that his mother will soon die. The mother won’t get out of the car. The film launched in Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight and picked up best director and best actor at the Shanghai International Film Festival.

Abinash Bikram Shah’s “Elephants in the Fog” won the Jury Prize in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard strand, the first Nepali film to make the festival’s official selection. The debut feature centers on Pilati, head of a kinnar, or third-gender, community in a village hemmed in by elephant forest, who takes over the hunt for a missing girl when police won’t help.

Venice supplies four competition titles. Phuttiphong Aroonpheng’s Horizons entry “The Burning Giants” follows a young policeman who begins to doubt a government operation that closes off a forest and moves out its Indigenous Karen residents after a strange white smoke starts burning people. Michelle Zhou drew on her own life for her debut “Big Little Things,” also from Horizons, in which a woman takes a hired fake boyfriend back to Harbin for the Lunar New Year holiday to keep her girlfriend secret from her mother. It won Venice’s Premio Autrici Under 40 prize for young female directors and has four Golden Horse nominations.

Iranian filmmaker Ali Asgari’s “A Bit of Light,” from Venice’s main competition, tracks a Tehran doctor who loses his license for treating injured protesters and plans to kill himself. Amie Song’s debut “Gu Shi,” made through Venice’s Biennale College Cinema program with Anocha Suwichakornpong as executive producer, wraps its politics in a fairy tale about a family hiding out in an isolated house wedged between forest and sea.

Two films come from Toronto. Korean director Yoon Dan-bi’s “The World Before,” from the Platform competition, centers on a 17-year-old girl on a southern island who is drawn to a childhood friend back home for his grandmother’s funeral. It earned a special mention in San Sebastian’s New Directors section. Filipino filmmaker John Torres’ first narrative feature “The Remotes,” which also played the New York Film Festival, is a neo-noir in which a widowed detective close to retirement connects a run of fatal road crashes to a voice app designed to retrain reckless drivers.

Singaporean director Priscilla Ang’s debut “Ah Girl,” set in 1994 and framed in 4:3, won the Youth Jury Award in Rotterdam’s Bright Future section and has three Golden Horse nominations. Rounding out the selection is “A Song From Beyond,” the fifth feature from Japan’s Sugita Kyoshi, whose “Haruhara-san’s Recorder” won the FIDMarseille Grand Prix. A photographer agrees to act in a student’s graduation film, only to find that her estranged father has been cast as the father.

Novelist Maha Harada’s directing debut “In My Father’s Room,” revealed as the opener earlier this month, will kick off the festival. Harada adapted it from one of her own short stories, and it stars Yu Aoi as a museum guard who receives an unfamiliar key from her estranged father, played by Issey Ogata, a month after his death. The film premiered in competition at San Sebastian, where it won the Fipresci Prize and the Ateneo Guipuzcoano Award.

Anthony Chen’s “We Are All Strangers” will close the event. The film completes the Singaporean director’s “Growing Up” trilogy, after “Ilo Ilo” and “Wet Season,” and centers on a hawker-stall owner and his son, 21, who both marry and end up sharing a small public housing flat. It was the first Singaporean film picked for the Berlinale’s main competition and is Singapore’s Oscar submission.

Both titles sit in the 12-film Special Screenings section. Korean auteur Hong Sang-soo’s 34th feature, the black-and-white “The Day She Returns,” arrives from Berlin’s Panorama, while Kogonada’s Hong Kong-set “Zi,” dedicated to the late composer Sakamoto Ryuichi, comes from Sundance’s NEXT section. Ann Hui’s 1981 Hong Kong New Wave thriller “The Story of Woo Viet,” starring a 25-year-old Chow Yun-fat, screens in the M+ 4K restoration that premiered in Venice Classics.

Poh Si Teng’s documentary “American Doctor,” about three U.S. volunteer physicians who treated the wounded in Gaza before lobbying the media and Congress, took the Hot Docs Audience Award after premiering in Sundance’s U.S. Documentary Competition. Japanese filmmaker Irie Yu’s documentary feature debut “The Day He Retires” will world premiere at the festival. It follows Takeishi Kenji, who left his job at 50 to open Fukaya Cinema in Saitama, as he hands the theater to a new generation at 76.

Lee will also be on screen in a double bill of Tsai’s two newest “Walker” films, the series running since 2012 in which he plays a present-day version of Tang dynasty monk Xuanzang, moving through cities around the world at a glacial crawl. “Dust,” the 11th chapter, was shot in San Sebastian and premiered at Venice. The 12th, “Night Journey,” takes place in the Czech town of Jihlava and is a Golden Horse nominee for best documentary short.

Jia Zhangke’s “Torino Shadow,” made at the invitation of Turin’s National Cinema Museum and first shown as a Cannes special screening, headlines a shorts program alongside work by younger directors. These include Carlo Francisco Manatad’s “And If Thuy Didn’t Exist,” a special mention recipient in Locarno’s shorts competition, and “The Bovine Comedy” from “A Useful Ghost” director Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke, which won Locarno’s Pardino d’Oro for best auteur short.

The Made in Japan sidebar has three titles. Yamanishi Tatsuya’s “Goodbye, Absence” and Sasaki Omoi’s “22nd Century Cat” will both world premiere in Tokyo. Xavier Tera’s debut “The Color of the Sun,” set in Okinawa in 2012 and lensed on 35mm by Sayombhu Mukdeeprom, won the Fipresci Prize in Venice’s Horizons section.

Screenings will take place at Yurakucho Asahi Hall, Marunouchi Piccadilly and Human Trust Cinema Yurakucho. Talents Tokyo 2026, held in cooperation with Berlinale Talents, will run in parallel at Vision Center Yurakucho and Yurakucho Asahi Square. The 25 films unveiled so far span three sections.

article_text:
It has been a remarkable year for the Hong Kong–born, Paris-based filmmaker and editor Mary Stephen. Her acclaimed first feature, Ombres de soie ( Shades of Silk , 1978), which she directed, acted in, and co-edited at 24 years old, has been restored and recently premiered at this year’s New York Film Festival in the Revivals section. A visually sumptuous and delicate tale of an unresolved relationship between two young Chinese women, the film is carried by elegant voiceover and entrancing cinematography that gracefully relate how memories and regrets linger.

Stephen’s early short films Labyrinthe (1973) and A Very Easy Death (1975) have also recently been restored, and she is currently traveling with her latest feature, Palimpsest: The Story of a Name —a deeply personal essay-documentary that investigates her Chinese family’s Western surname. Drawing from her father Henry’s meticulously maintained diaries and home-movie archive, and her mother Hilda’s writing career (she wrote poems under a pen name and doctored some of Henry’s journals), Stephen constructs a portrait of a family lineage riddled with coincidences and embellishments. The film elucidates how, as her parents ascended the social ladder in mid-century Hong Kong, a Western surname provided them—and her—advantages, which nevertheless came with compromises.

Stephen’s family immigrated to Canada when she was 15 years old. After finishing two years of film school at Concordia University in Montreal, she moved to Paris in 1976, whereafter she began a career in film editing. Stephen is most often associated with French New Wave filmmaker Éric Rohmer, as his chief editor and regular collaborator for over 20 years. In recent decades, she has edited numerous films by directors such as Ann Hui ( Love After Love , 2020), Du Haibin ( A Young Patriot , 2015), and Lixin Fan ( Last Train Home , 2009), and she frequently mentors young filmmakers in her free time.

I interviewed Stephen during NYFF at the New York Public Library for the Performing Arts. We discussed her early editing career in Paris, the making of her first feature, and the inspirations behind Palimpsest.

What was your experience of working as an editor in French cinema?

I didn’t really set out to be an editor. I was studying in Paris for one year, and decided to drop out of the program to make films because it was very theoretical. That year, we were allowed to take other courses in the French universities, and I found one taught by Éric Rohmer. I wanted to stay in France, and I needed some money to do that. Rohmer asked me to be the editing assistant for The Aviator’s Wife (1981). The editor was Cécile Decugis, who edited Godard’s Breathless (1960). So I was very happy to do that. When I was training back in Canada, we had to do everything—editing, sound, image. I think if at the time Néstor Alemendros (who shot many of Rohmer’s films) had needed an assistant, maybe now I’d be on camera, who knows? It was that kind of stroke of destiny, but it ended up that I loved editing.

What was the atmosphere like when you were working with Rohmer and other filmmakers of the time?

It was very much a clan. There were just a few of us working with him, and we almost never got out of that circle. Whenever we were doing some work, we would help each other out, and would always pay each other. His whole working method was like a family. With the actors as well—a few key actors—we would have tea at his office every afternoon. It was never really just “work.”

What did you learn about the editing process from Cécile Decugis?

As an assistant, I was in the room with Éric and Cécile where they physically cut the film. I would see the process—at what point they decided to cut, how the collaboration went, how they negotiated with each other and respected each other. That’s the kind of process you can’t learn unless you’re working on-site. For The Aviator’s Wife , Rohmer shot on 16mm and we conformed it to 35mm. That took meticulous work. It served as a learning process as well, because you had to be very precise.

That’s something that I realize makes a difference in my work today. In digital cutting, you don’t have to be very precise, and I can’t emphasize enough about the one-frame difference—just one frame makes a big difference. I try to get my students today to learn that discipline of getting to the exact cut point.

You’ve described Ombres de soie , your first feature, as an homage to Marguerite Duras’s India Song (1975). Could you speak about the circumstances around the production of the film?

Before India Song , I was already very much in love with Hiroshima mon amour (1959), which was also written by Marguerite Duras. Even in Canada, when I was in film school, I had parts of the script pasted on my wall, because I really loved the language, the way she described things.

There’s a Chinese expression about how young girls, before even knowing sadness, would write very sad verses—it was trendy to do that. I was particularly attached to that poetic, melancholic writing before I even knew what it was about. That was the first driving force—I wanted to write something like that.

For the production, we didn’t have any money. We were living in the Cité Universitaire, the international students’ residences in Paris. Each nationality had a house in this complex. My partner and I were living in the Canadian house, which had a huge salon that became the place where the girls in the film dance the tango. The American house had a beautiful outdoor terrace with tables—that’s where the dance sequence at the beginning was shot. A major part of the film was set in the Southeast Asian students’ house.

It’s not out of some egotistical exhibitionism that I starred in most of my films. It was because we couldn’t find anybody else. At the time, we had to find two Asian women. We’re talking about 48, 49 years ago in Paris. There weren’t a lot of Asians. The cheapest person to hire was me [ laughs ]! And Sandy Brouwer, who was in our program—she’s half Thai, half Dutch.

I really admire the way this film is made with voiceovers, and how sound and image—and bodies and voices—are divided. It gives this sense of disembodiment that beautifully reflects the themes of displacement, longing, and misunderstanding. Can you speak about this formal separation?

Again, it was for economic reasons! That was quite directly influenced by Marguerite Duras’s films. One of the things Rohmer taught his students, and was still teaching them many years later, was the way Duras had made her movies for practically nothing. I loved the India Song soundtrack. I played it over and over again—this hypnotic quality of voices and the mix of languages. The voiceover enabled me to make this film. We didn’t have the money to make synchronized sound.

How did you make the music for Ombres de soie ?

I wanted Billie Holiday’s “Blue Moon,” but we couldn’t afford the rights. This musician who ran a company providing royalty-free music said he would make the soundtrack for us. I said I would write the lyrics, and he knew a singer who could record it. We did it all in one go in a Montreal studio.

From when I was very young in Hong Kong, I used to write little poems and song lyrics all the time. I loved to do that. I did that later for my film The Memory of Water (2018) as well, where I used three languages to write a song. I tend to think of language as music, and like working with them as musical elements separately from speech.

I’ve read you began research for Palimpsest about 20 years ago. How did this film develop?

My Chinese friend, a Hong Kong writer, told me that Virginia Woolf’s maiden name was Stephen. That sparked a scenario in my head—I’d love to make a film where two branches of Stephens come together to make a reflection on what a name is about, whether it can change a destiny, what kind of connotation and expectation comes from it. I started researching Virginia Woolf’s story and thinking about how to connect it with my mother’s writings and my father’s story.

I knew that my father filmed a lot. I’d seen bits and pieces, but never all of the home-movie footage, because it wasn’t digitized. It was all stored at my sister’s place. Every time I went to Canada, she would ask me to take a few cans back because she didn’t know what to do with them. I had some digitized with money from a Canadian prize, and the rest at a place in Paris, and it turned out to be amazing—the colors were really beautiful. It was only then that I started to look at everything he had shot. Not only did they feel like period pieces, but he was making movie shots. He was editing himself, doing shot/reverse shots, some animated titling, stop-motion—all in those days.

Palimpsest seems like a significant accumulation of your long-standing interests in language, migration, personal histories, and the idea of place.

Somehow, for some strange reason, it was appropriate to make this film at this stage. It’s even more interesting given that my other films have also reemerged at the same time, and I’m able to see them as a whole. I think it’s necessary to rewrite your own past. In today’s practices of therapy and healing, the path is not just about understanding or digging up your past, but learning how to rewrite it. You have to redirect the energy somehow, because some people get stuck there.

article_text:
W e just had Resident Evil , Zach Cregger’s giddy, nasty, devilishly fun spin on Capcom’s popular zombie franchise. It gave us renewed hope (after Sonic the Hedgehog, The Last of Us and Fallout) that video game adaptations could be good, actually.

But now here comes Street Fighter, a garish and incoherent mess that amuses in fits and starts but barely improves on the Mortal Kombat movies before it, crushing those hopes in its atomic suplex.

Fans certainly won’t mind. They’ve kept the box office’s life bar in the green for these one-on-one fighter adaptations going all the way back to the disastrous 1994 Street Fighter movie starring Jean-Claude Van Damme and his $10,000-a-week coke problem . They’ll happily tolerate how the new Street Fighter, like those Mortal Kombat movies, can barely string together a cohesive plot, which has clearly been pencilled in as an afterthought between rounds of combat in yet another tournament-style narrative. None of that will matter because they’re just here for the dopamine hits by way of nostalgia.

To that end, the movie exhaustively rolls out all the iconic characters and moves from the games – like Sumo warrior E Honda’s hundred-hand slap or military bro Guile’s flash kick – not to mention some at-times striking anime flashback sequences and a bevy of pop culture ephemera from its early-90s setting. Grainy, UHF quality MTV video segments show Ken (Noah Centineo) to be a self-destructive New Kids on the Block-era celebrity party boy with flashy blond curls, while the needle drops bring back bygone hits like MC Hammer’s 2 Legit 2 Quit and Montell Jordan’s This Is How We Do It.

It’s all about keeping us pampered in those fond memories from our pubescent childhoods, including bits that bring back the way us preteen boys ogled the 16-bit version of hypersexualized Chun-Li. She’s played in the movie by the lively and commanding Callina Liang, who enters the frame thighs first and unfortunately plays the only character tasked with a gratuitous slow-motion shower scene.

Liang doesn’t let that stuff drag down her performance, which is formidable, while her physicality during fight scenes is genuinely impressive. She’s one of the handful who bring some modest pleasures to the overcrowded mess. WWE wrestler Cody Rhodes, wearing a cartoonish trapezoid blond wig as Guile, is genuinely funny in the way he barks pleasantries and threats in equal measure. Indian movie star Vidyut Jammwal, who is trained in the ancient martial art Kalaripayattu, brings captivating authenticity and hypnotic movements to his all-too-brief scenes as yoga priest Dhalsim. Even controversial comic and manosphere podcaster Andrew Schulz gives a convincing performance worthy of an essay, playing Ken’s manager, who capitalizes on his bro’s brawn while coddling his wounded ego.

But the likable performances get buried in a movie that often feels like it was made on a six-button control pad. Street Fighter is a barrage of character introductions and story arcs lifted from the games and animated spin-offs, colliding into one another in a way that makes a relatively linear plot (it’s a freakin’ fight tournament!) confusing. Did Vega edit this with his Wolverine-like claw hands?

The movie’s most amusing fight arrives early, with Ken and Ryu (Andrew Koji) reunited in a hotel room after a years-long fallout, lured back together for a world championship tournament that the movie’s villain M Bison organized for nefarious purposes. Ken furiously takes wild swings at Ryu. Flying kicks miss the mark. Roundhouses hit nothing but air. Ryu quickly and calmly out-maneuvers, blocking with a pillow and then hilariously slipping the pillow below Ken’s head to catch his wipeout, or tiptoeing away from Ken while planted in a sofa seat. It’s a standout scene that really does feel like it belongs to another, smarter movie.

Elsewhere, during a matchup between Ken and boxer Balrog (played by rapper 50 Cent), Sakurai learns the right lessons from Martin Scorsese’s Raging Bull, quick cutting between flashy hits and slow-motion impacts, the sloppy mix of blood and drool flying from Ken’s mouth hanging in the air long enough to appreciate its viscosity.

And then there’s Liang’s Chun-Li, whose legwork delivers spectacular action, while her character tends to be the one dragging others down to earth with quick, frank, intermittently funny verbal jabs. She’s the grounded one, standing 10 toes down in purpose and principle. Whenever Ken or Ryu start emoting or waxing philosophical like Steven Seagal or Van Damme in those movies that inspire Street Fighter, Liang’s Chun-Li calls out in the most basic terms how stupid they sound.

There’s several knowing winks at the fans like this, guarding against criticism by owning up to how silly this all is, which would land better if the movie ever rose above the stuff it’s making fun of. Instead, Street Fighter is satisfied punching down on itself, and everything that’s cringe about the 90s, while happily being stuck there, in the past, so it could pretend that this is as good as it gets for video game adaptations.

We know better.

Street Fighter is out in Australian cinemas now and in the UK and US on 16 October

‘On paper, both countries agree that smacking your child is illegal’: Romanian journalist Andrei Popoviciu

When Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord was shown in Romania as a one-day preview this June, the reception was extraordinary. Across 53 towns and 96 cinemas, the film reportedly pulled in over 40,000 viewers in a single night, a number arthouse cinema rarely sees in Romania. But the response here had little to do with cinema. It felt instead like a reopening of a familiar fault line about the clash of values within the EU itself.

The film echoes events from 2015, when the five children of Marius and Ruth Bodnariu, a Pentecostal couple from Romania living in Norway – part of a Neo-Protestant minority long viewed with suspicion in Orthodox Romania – were removed from their home by Barnevernet, Norway’s child welfare authority, amid concerns over possible corporal punishment and religious indoctrination.

The fallout in Romania stretched on for months, with diplomatic friction, public demonstrations and constant media coverage. The children were eventually returned, and the Bodnarius later resettled in Romania. Mungiu doesn’t retell the story beat for beat, but Romanian viewers had no trouble recognising where it came from.

What divided viewers here was what the film did with a well-known story. Some have called it “dangerously confusing”, raising questions about abuse, integration and belief without taking a clear position. Others counter that its stance is embedded in form, in how sympathy is distributed, which characters get interiority and which are reduced to function.

To some, it’s a brave critique of dogmatic liberalism, while to others, it dilutes a clear moral boundary on corporal punishment while extending undue warmth to religious conservatism. At its most charged, the debate spills into a broader anxiety about whether the EU can sustain its own contradictions.

That tension surfaced again weeks later, when a viral video of a Romanian mother mistreating her daughter in public reignited the same split online (many defended her as exercising necessary discipline, others condemned her outright) suggesting attitudes here may be shifting, but unevenly.

It’s worth pausing on how narrow the legal gap between the two countries actually is, because the film’s reception treats it as a chasm. Romania criminalised corporal punishment in 2004, Norway in 1987. On paper, both already agree smacking your child is illegal, but the real distance is between law and belief.

A UN human rights body recently noted that despite the ban, Romania still needs to shift the mindset of parents who believe corporal punishment works better than the alternative. The Orthodox church, meanwhile, has never fully shed a folk theology in which strict discipline raises a righteous child, even as doctrine and law increasingly say otherwise.

What’s notable is how little agreement there is about what the film actually endorses. Some say the supporting characters – social workers, lawyers, neighbours – are too thin to carry the moral weight asked of them. Others accuse Mungiu of stacking the deck, giving the Christian-conservative family warmth while leaving Norwegian institutions cold and procedural.

Mungiu has spoken of challenging “leftwing fundamentalism”, a phrase conservatives have seized on as vindication, though he has equally condemned its rightwing counterpart. Defenders counter that a director sympathetic to victims must be willing to defend a conservative minority in a progressive society just as he’d defend a progressive one surrounded by conservatives, since majorities of any stripe tend to need an “other” to demonise.

Some critics have said that intent stops mattering once a film reaches an audience, so whatever Mungiu meant by refusing to pick a side, the dramatic architecture produces sympathy for the family almost by default.

My own sense is that Fjord is a film about whether a system convinced of its own good intentions can imagine being wrong. It’s the same reflex found in churches, homes and government offices from Oslo to Bucharest and across the polarised world we live in – the certainty that one’s side only ever needs vindication, never correction.

‘Norway sees itself as a country that takes the rights of children more seriously than others’: Norwegian writer Magnus Nome

The flipside of Norway’s often lauded “trust society” can manifest as a naive belief in the wisdom of its institutions, but there have long been discussions about Barnevernet, the child protection service: an imperfect system consisting of fallible humans, wielding the power to reach into the inner sanctum of the family.

Systemic mistakes have been made: the European court of human rights ruled against Norway in multiple cases between 2018 and 2021. In a key case, the ECHR found the system in violation by not prioritising family reunification, treating an initial foster home placement as permanent from the start instead of working towards reunification with the biological mother. In another ruling against Barnevernet, the court criticised placing the son of a Muslim mother in an Evangelical Christian family, despite the mother’s request for her child to grow up in an environment reflecting his cultural and religious background.

The former case resulted in a series of Norwegian supreme court rulings that made a reunification goal mandatory, ensured a higher level of minimum contact for parents and raised the threshold for forced adoption. The latter resulted in a revision in the country’s Child Welfare Act, mandating active steps to preserve a child’s cultural, religious and linguistic identity during foster placements. Fjord is a portrait of the system prior to these changes.

A serious public debate about these issues has often been hard to accomplish, partly because discussion of specific cases is inevitably based on one-sided information, as Barnevernet adheres to strict confidentiality for the sake of the children involved. We only get the parents’ version, allowing them to form the public narrative, flipping the power dynamic. At the same time it relieves Barnevernet of having to counter concrete allegations of wrongdoing.

There has long been a deep vein of harsh criticism directed at Barnevernet, reaching wide and far; social media groups numbering tens of thousands of furious members, more or less full-time activists (often with personal experience) and street protests in more than a dozen countries. It’s a surprising amount of international commotion around the social services of a small nation.

Within the activist circles, the critiques frequently cross from principled concern into radical conspiracy theories: there are claims of adoptions for profit, organ harvesting and organised sex trade of minors, and accusations of being an ultraliberal indoctrination project, or a state-sanctioned eugenics programme. As a result, social workers have experienced harassment and threats.

While the wild conspiracy theories have been debunked, most recently by the major newspaper VG, the reach of dramatic tales far surpasses that of well-documented refutations – not least when amplified by both foreign media with little local insight, and propaganda outlets such as the Russian RT, always happy to present “evidence” of the degeneracy of the liberal west.

Such rampant misinformation ( not limited to Norway ) can at times hinder necessary debate, with criticism automatically assumed to originate from cranks. But most agree, including within Barnevernet itself, that an ongoing debate about the system is necessary and healthy.

One can see Fjord, and the issue it portrays, as conservatism against liberal leftism, powerless individuals against an arrogant system, or a conflict between prioritising parents’ rights over those of the children.

Most parents, myself among them, will insist they know what’s best for their own children better than any arm of the state – but some of those parents will also know of families with dangerously unfit parents that hold exactly the same opinion. Norway sees itself as a country that takes the rights of children more seriously than others, aware that while taking action carries the risk of harm, passive inaction and automatic acquiescence to parents can be equally damaging.

Fjord may not be entirely objective or tell the complete story, but it’s a more nuanced work than the previous cinematic depiction of Barnevernet, Mrs Chatterjee vs Norway – a sensationalist Bollywood drama based on a mother’s account. To balance the film with a sympathetic portrayal of the dilemmas faced by social workers, the award-winning dramedy TV series Pernille, whose eponymous main character works in Barnevernet, is available on Netflix.
